newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: First contract arrives at UN for Iraqi oil.
newsitem.headline: First contract arrives at UN for Iraqi oil.

text.p: Moments after the limited oil sales plan for Iraq came into effect, one contract to purchase oil from Iraq was received a U.N. headquarters, spokeswoman Sylvana Foa said.
She knew no details about the contract that oil experts or overseers by the United Nations were now studying.
"Three overseers were staring at the fax machine at midnight and one contract came in," said told Reuters.
Two of the four overseers are needed to approve each contract which is to fall within a pricing formula approved by the Security Council's sanctions committee.

The United Nations on Monday authorized the start of a long-delayed "oil-for-food" deal with Iraq, enabling Baghdad to make a limited return to the world oil market for the first time since its 1990 invasion of Kuwait. The plan went into effect early on Tuesday.

Under the plan, concluded in May but held up by disputes over implementation, Iraq will be able to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy food, medicine and other humanitarian goods after six years of sanctions.
But the deal is subject to close U.N. monitoring. If all goes well, the Security Council may renew the deal when the initial six months expire.

At current oil prices, Iraq will be able to export slightly under 600,000 barrels of oil per day (bpd). In 1989, before the Gulf War, Iraq produced over 3.5 million bpd of oil and exported 2.3 million bpd.
The proceeds from the oil sale will be placed in an escrow account in the New York branch of the Banque Nationale de Paris.
Some $1.32 billion of each $2 billion from the oil sales will go for humanitarian supplies, including $260 million earmarked for goods for the largely Kurdish-populated north.

Of the remainder, $600 million will be funneled into a U.N. compensation fund to pay Gulf War reparations. Another $20 million will go to the cash-strapped U.N. weapons commission while administrative and operational costs account for most of the rest.

These include the stationing of some 150 U.N. inspectors in Iraq to ensure that food and other supplies reach all sectors of the population, not just those favored by the Iraqi government. Another 32 inspectors from Lloyd's Register will check on the import of the humanitarian goods.

In addition, 14 U.N. inspectors from the Dutch-based Saybolt company, already in place, will monitor the outflow of Iraqi oil at three locations -- at a pipeline metering station at Zakho, on the Iraq-Turkish border; at the Turkish terminal of Ceyhan; and at the Gulf port of Mina al-Bakr.
Oil flow into Mina Bakr is expected to be delayed until the end of the week when a malfunctioning meter will be replaced, according to Gulf shipping sources.

A Turkish oil official said that no Iraqi oil had arrived at the Ceyhan terminal, hours after the offical Iraqi News Agency said President Saddam Hussein had pressed the button to resume Iraqi exports to the world from its northern city of Kirkuk.
Turkish television had said that Iraq was not able to send oil because of electrical fault at its pumping station in the Kirkuk.
